title: Catch a SyntaxError
description:
Source instruction (Exercises: Day 15, item 1): "Open you python interactive shell and try all the examples covered in this section."

SyntaxError example from the section: `print 'hello world'` raises a SyntaxError ("As you can see we made a syntax error because we forgot to enclose the string with parenthesis and Python already suggests the solution."). Fixing it to `print('hello world')` runs without error.

Python-Gym adaptation: implement as `check_syntax(code)`, executing the given code string with `exec()` and returning "OK: no SyntaxError" if it runs cleanly, or a string "SyntaxError: <message>" describing the caught SyntaxError if it doesn't, instead of letting the exception crash the program.
examples:
check_syntax("print 'hello world'") -> "SyntaxError: Missing parentheses in call to 'print'. Did you mean print(...)? (<string>, line 1)"
check_syntax("print('hello world')") -> 'OK: no SyntaxError'
hints: A SyntaxError is raised while Python parses code, so to catch one at runtime you need to actually run the given string as code, not just inspect it.
The built-in exec() function compiles and runs a string as Python code, and raises SyntaxError immediately if the string isn't valid Python.
Wrap exec(code) in try/except SyntaxError, and in the except branch build the return string as an f-string starting with 'SyntaxError: ' followed by the caught exception object.
expected_behavior: Executes the given code string with exec(). If it runs without error, returns "OK: no SyntaxError". If exec() raises a SyntaxError, catches it and returns a descriptive string in the form "SyntaxError: <message>" instead of letting the exception propagate.

hidden_tests.expected: "SyntaxError: Missing parentheses in call to 'print'. Did you mean print(...)? (<string>, line 1)"
hidden_tests.label: bad syntax: unparenthesized print statement

explanation: exec() parses and runs the given string as Python code. An unparenthesized print statement like `print 'hello world'` is not valid Python 3 syntax, so exec() raises a SyntaxError before any code runs; the except block catches it and turns it into a descriptive return value instead of crashing.
